title: Model merging: weighted, SLERP, task arithmetic

questions.q: What is the primary computational advantage of model merging (creating a 'model soup') over using an ensemble of models?
options: It requires less VRAM and compute during inference because it results in a single checkpoint.
It allows for real-time fine-tuning during the inference process.
It eliminates the need for a base model entirely.
It automatically corrects hallucinations without any manual intervention.
questions.answer: It requires less VRAM and compute during inference because it results in a single checkpoint.
questions.why: The lesson states that unlike an ensemble, which doubles VRAM and compute by running multiple models, a merged model is a single checkpoint where you pay the cost once at merge time and then just run one model.

questions.q: In the context of Task Arithmetic, how is the 'task vector' defined?
options: The sum of the weights of the fine-tuned model and the base model.
The difference between the fine-tuned model and the base model ($W_{fine} - W_{base}$).
The average of the weights of two different fine-tuned models.
The L2 norm of the fine-tuned model's weights.
questions.answer: The difference between the fine-tuned model and the base model ($W_{fine} - W_{base}$).
questions.why: The lesson explicitly defines the task vector $V$ as $V = W_{fine} - W_{base}$, describing it as the difference between the fine-tuned model and the base model.

questions.q: Why is SLERP (Spherical Linear Interpolation) often preferred over linear interpolation for merging models where weight magnitude carries semantic meaning?
options: It is computationally cheaper than linear interpolation.
It preserves the magnitude (norm) of the weights, avoiding the 'shrinkage' effect toward the origin.
It assumes the path between weights is a straight line through the center of the sphere.
It automatically scales the output to zero to prevent overfitting.
questions.answer: It preserves the magnitude (norm) of the weights, avoiding the 'shrinkage' effect toward the origin.
questions.why: The lesson explains that linear interpolation can cause the resulting vector to have a smaller norm (shrink toward the origin), while SLERP, when scaled to the average norm, perfectly preserves the magnitude of the weights.

questions.q: According to the lab results, what was the norm of the SLERP merged vector, and how did it compare to the average of the parent norms?
questions.answer: The norm was 3.49621, which was exactly equal to the average of the parent norms.
questions.why: The lab results show `RESULT norm_slerp = 3.49621`. The analysis states that the average of the parent norms is $(3.61211 + 3.38031) / 2 = 3.49621$, confirming that SLERP perfectly preserved the magnitude.

questions.q: What is a common mistake when using SLERP that can result in a model producing black images?
options: Using a scalar weight ($\alpha$) greater than 1.
Forgetting to scale the unit vector output back to the average norm of the inputs.
Adding the task vectors instead of interpolating the full weights.
Using a base model that has not been fine-tuned.
questions.answer: Forgetting to scale the unit vector output back to the average norm of the inputs.
questions.why: The 'Common mistakes' section states that the raw SLERP output is a unit vector, and if you forget to scale it back to the average norm, the model will have near-zero weights and produce black images.
